name: Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports
title: Bias Audits, Accessibility Checks, and Incident Reports
answer: Bias audits, accessibility checks, and incident reports are three routine checks that keep AI use honest over time. The bias check looks at whether a tool treats groups of students differently, the accessibility check makes sure tools students must use work with screen readers, captions, and keyboard navigation, and the incident report gives staff and students a simple way to report when an AI tool gets something wrong, shows bias, or causes harm. They matter because they turn fairness, access, and harm reporting into ongoing review rather than one time approval.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: The idea is to build three repeating checks into how a school reviews and lives with AI tools. A bias check compares who gets flagged, placed, or disciplined before and after a tool arrives, because research on test score prediction found that balanced groups in the data did not guarantee fair predictions. An accessibility check asks whether any tool students must use works with screen readers, captions, and keyboard navigation and meets the federal standard described earlier. An incident report gives staff and students a shared way to flag errors, bias, or harm, with a shared form reviewed monthly as a starting point. Together these checks solve the problem of AI use drifting out of sight after approval, when no one is regularly asking whether the tool is fair, usable, or causing harm.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the bias check means comparing who gets flagged, placed, or disciplined before and after a tool arrives. The accessibility check can be part of the approval review, and the technology director can ask vendors for an accessibility report. The incident report can begin as a shared form reviewed monthly, as long as someone reads it and the district publishes what it fixed. Students can help with all three checks, and a small student advisory group that meets each quarter with school leaders will spot problems adults miss. The text does not give separate grade band steps, so these routines apply across the school rather than by year group.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites research on test score prediction which found that simply including balanced groups in the data did not guarantee fair predictions, so the check has to look at results, not just inputs (Li et al., 2026). It also describes one two year project in which an advisory board of former students and experts helped improve a high school AI curriculum, and student learning gains were larger in the second year (Moore et al., 2026). The text does not give a formal evidence label for these checks, and it does not report other studies, figures, or findings beyond those two citations.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on each check. A bias check cannot rely only on balanced inputs, because fair predictions are not guaranteed and the results must be examined. A tool that shuts out a student with a disability is not ready, however good it is for everyone else, so accessibility is a condition for tools students must use. An incident report only works if someone reads it and the district publishes what it fixed, which keeps a person responsible for review and follow up. Students can help spot problems, but the decisions about vendor accessibility reports, tool approval, and what gets fixed stay with adults such as the technology director and school leaders.
